newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Red Cross says clashes won't halt aid to North.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross says clashes won't halt aid to North.

text.p: The South Korean Red Cross will offer more food aid to hunger-stricken North Korea despite a border clash earlier this week, a Seoul Red Cross spokesman said on Friday.
The South Korean organisation sent a message to the North, saying it had accepted the North's demand that Red Cross talks on food supplies be held in Beijing next Wednesday, he said.
"Food aid will continue," the spokesman told Reuters when asked if Wednesday's shooting across the border would have any impact on shipments of aid to the North.

South Korea and the U.S.-led United Nations Command have protested to Pyongyang over the fierce exchange of fire at the Demilitarised Zone, which followed an intrusion by North Korean soldiers' across the demarcation line bisecting the DMZ.
The DMZ, set up as a buffer zone under an armistice agreement that ended the 1950-53 Korean War, is now the world's last Cold War flashpoint.

The South Korean Red Cross, which is due to complete shipments of 50,000 tonnes of corn and other food to North Korea this month, plans to offer additional relief supplies in Beijing next week, the spokesman said.
"We have more promises of donations by civic groups," he said. The Red Cross is the only legal channel for private aid from South Korea to the North.
No exact size of additional aid was given, but it would be "tens of thousands of tonnes of food and possibly fertiliser", he added.
The South Korean Red Cross proposed last week to hold talks in the Korean peninsula on July 22, but the North countered on Tuesday that the meeting be held in Beijing on July 23.
The 50,000 tonnes of food supplies were agreed in May following a round of talks in Beijing, the first between the two sides for almost five years.
The relief supplies via the Red Cross are on top of $16 million worth of donations made by the Seoul government in response to an aid appeal by the U.N. World Food Programme.
Following the latest urgent appeal by the WFP, Washington pledged $27 million in food aid, bringing to $52 million its contribution for the year.
U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the shooting incident would have no effect on U.S. food aid.
U.S. and South Korean officials said the border shooting underlined the importance of starting four-nation peace talks between the two Koreas, the United States and China.
Senior officials of the four countries are due to meet in New York on August 5 to prepare for the talks.
Floods that devastated much of the North's farmland and industrial bases in 1995 and 1996 exacerbated already severe food shortages.
